_about: Inputs for scripts/build_demo_data.py. The research_notes/ paths are build-time inputs from the project's local, git-ignored working archive (see scripts/README.md); readers find the summary results in evaluation/. The status and sources strings below are shown on the demo page.

status.title: Checked, and how
items: Form. The city-wide graph passes the OpenSidewalks schema validator published by the Taskar Center for Accessible Technology (python-osw-validation 0.5.0) with zero errors, and so does the Brownsville extract drawn here. The validator checks form. It does not check the schema's topology rules, and the data departs from them where OpenStreetMap joins crossings straight to sidewalks. It does not check whether the data matches the street.

Where a surveyed ramp serves a crossing. 200 crossings were rated remotely over the city's 2018 aerial photographs. Of the 166 crossings that the 16 ft (5 m) rule passes, the raters judged that 164 have a surveyed ramp placed to serve both ends (98.8%). The raters were language-model programs (Anthropic Claude models, exact versions not recorded) following a written protocol, not people. Two separate runs agreed on 96% of the 132 crossing ends both rated. That shows the raters are consistent. It does not show that the ramps are there today or that anyone can use them. No crossing was visited.

The route search. This page's routes match Unweaver, the open routing engine the profile was adapted from. On 840 route requests in Brownsville the two agree every time on whether a route exists, and all 826 routes found by both have the same length to within 3 ft (1 m). On 514 more requests across the city they also agree every time on whether a route exists.

Against OpenRouteService. 362 of the 420 Brownsville test trips are compared here: the ones where both route finders start and end at the same places, to within 82 ft (25 m). 205 of the 362 start at a subway entrance, and none of those is shown under Routes. On the 362 trips, this graph and OpenRouteService's wheelchair profile (plain OpenStreetMap data, 10% incline limit, 6 cm or 2.4 in curb height limit) both find a route every time. They take the same route on 130 trips and different routes on 232. 151 of OpenRouteService's 362 routes (41.7%) use a crossing with no surveyed ramp within 16 ft (5 m) of one end. At these crossings OpenStreetMap either has no curb record or has one that OpenRouteService 10.0.1 does not treat as a barrier, such as a curb marked as raised (kerb=raised). 76 of the 362 routes pass over a curb marked that way.

What the disagreements look like from above. 48 places across the city where the two route finders part were drawn over the city's March 2024 aerial photographs. Language-model programs (Anthropic Claude models, exact versions not recorded) rated them, following a written protocol, and were not told why each place was chosen. Where OpenRouteService's route had been flagged as running in the roadway, the photograph agreed at 10 of 12 places. At the 11 crossings flagged for a missing ramp, the photograph never showed ramps at both ends. It showed one or none at 3 and could not tell at 8. At 15 cm (6 in) per pixel a curb ramp is rarely visible, so this check cannot confirm the ramp data. A second run rated 24 of the sheets again without seeing the first ratings, and agreed on the kind of place at 23. No person rated the sheets.

status.title: Where this graph does worse
items: Outside Brownsville it finds far fewer routes. When each trip's start and end are moved to the nearest mapped path, its wheelchair profile completes 91% of random trips in Brooklyn and 51% in the Bronx, where OpenRouteService completes 97% to 99%. A missing route can be a real barrier or a gap in the data, and this page cannot tell which.

It may refuse crossings that have ramps. Across Brooklyn, OpenStreetMap mappers tagged a lowered or flush curb at 1,893 of the 3,394 crossing ends (55.8%) where the survey has no ramp within 16 ft (5 m). Some of those are likely ramps built after the survey.
It does not read what OpenStreetMap records about surface, smoothness or places marked as not usable by wheelchair (wheelchair=no). OpenRouteService does.
Where OpenStreetMap has no separately drawn sidewalk, this graph has no route. OpenRouteService falls back to the roadway, which is a choice a rider may or may not want.

This graph has no ferry edges. With no wheelchair limits at all, OpenRouteService run on this graph completes 82.1% of random Manhattan trips, against 100% on plain OpenStreetMap. 349 of the 358 trips it loses have one end on Governors Island, Liberty Island or Ellis Island, which are reached by ferry.

It allows a steeper slope downhill (10%) than uphill (8.3%). Many people find steep downhill slopes risky, so this is a choice you may disagree with. The limits apply to every short stretch, so a noisy LiDAR reading on one short stretch can close a route.

status.title: Not checked
items: Nothing on this page has been checked on the ground. Nobody has measured a ramp with a level or traveled one of these routes for this project. A field audit would be needed to do that.
This project has not compared the survey's slopes with a hand measurement.
978 of the 2,363 surveyed ramps here are at corners DOT lists as rebuilt since the survey. Their slopes and status may describe ramps that are gone, and nothing here says how the new ramps measure.
Clear width past poles, trees and stoops, surface condition, the lip at the gutter, ponding, construction and snow are not in the data.
Whether a subway entrance has steps or an elevator is not in the data, so no trip shown under Routes starts at a subway entrance. 210 of the 420 test trips counted above do.
No wheelchair user, community organization or disability organization has reviewed this page, the data or the wheelchair profile. The Disclaimer says the same.
The imagery ratings were done by language-model programs following written protocols. No person rated the sheets.
The page passes automated accessibility checks (axe-core and pa11y, zero violations) and a keyboard pass. It has not been tested by a screen-reader user.
